idiom_name: trait factory with abstract type members (collections use scala.collection.Factory)
implementation_notes: A Scala trait declares one creation method per product kind, and each family is an object or class implementing it; abstract type members let a family pin the concrete product types so the compiler keeps them coherent, which is the standard Tour-of-Scala answer to 'abstract factory with types'. The standard library ships the same idea for collections as scala.collection.Factory / IterableFactory / BuildFrom, where a factory value is passed implicitly to control what a transformation builds. In Scala 3 a `given` of the factory replaces explicit passing when selection is contextual; prefer that over global objects when tests need a different family. For families with many product kinds, split into multiple traits (e.g., ButtonFactory, SliderFactory) and compose them via mixin or delegation rather than one wide trait.
pitfalls: Two givens of the same factory type make implicit search ambiguous or silently pick the wrong family; scope them explicitly or use a named instance.
object factories are process-wide singletons - stateful configuration must be constructor parameters on a class factory instead.

Abstract type members make product types path-dependent: clients must retain the factory path or use a type parameter/type projection, so expose stable abstract product traits when callers do not need the concrete family types.
Implicit scope rules mean a factory given in a test scope may not be visible where expected; prefer explicit `given f: WidgetFactory = MyFactory` to implicit resolution for production-critical code.
